paper.title: Improving Web Security through Machine Learning: A Feature-Based Methodology for Detecting Phishing URLs
paper.authors: Reem Alzubi, Tariq Bishtawi, Hassan Kassem

key_idea: The paper benchmarks Random Forest against Decision Tree, SVM, and XGBoost classifiers on lexical, host-based, and content-based URL features, and finds that ensemble methods -- particularly Random Forest -- consistently outperform individual and linear classifiers for phishing URL detection.
research_gap: The paper reports strong aggregate accuracy metrics, but like most classic phishing-ML papers it does not give an end user or analyst any way to see which features drove an individual prediction, and it does not ship an interactive tool a non-technical person could use to check a suspicious link in real time.
how_this_extends_it: PhishGuard AI implements the paper's core methodology (URL feature extraction feeding a Random Forest classifier, benchmarked against a linear baseline) using a 20-feature lexical-only subset chosen for zero network dependency and near-instant predictions. It closes the paper's explainability gap by wrapping every prediction in a SHAP TreeExplainer that produces threshold-aware, plain-English reasons, and packages the whole pipeline as a live, deployable dashboard rather than an offline experiment.
future_work: Add the paper's host-based and content-based feature families (WHOIS/domain age, DNS records, page HTML analysis) behind an optional 'deep scan' toggle to approach the paper's reported accuracy ceiling.
Replace SQLite with a managed Postgres instance for durable scan history across deployments.
Package the analysis endpoint as a browser extension for real-time link checking.
Track prediction drift over time as phishing URL patterns evolve, with scheduled retraining.
Cross-check flagged URLs against live threat-intelligence feeds (PhishTank, OpenPhish) as an additional signal alongside VirusTotal.
